purpose: machine-readable ontology for selecting, applying, and honestly reporting statistical inference methods (frequentist estimation and testing, Bayesian inference, likelihood, resampling, power, multiplicity control, effect sizes, and model selection) as evaluable work units, as a subdomain node of quantitative/statistical analysis and causal inference for a knowledge-searcher meta-KB.
assumptions: Statistical Inference is modeled as a subdomain of quantitative/statistical analysis and causal inference.
Nodes are concrete, evaluable inference work units, decision areas, or validity/reporting controls.
No observed dataset or experimental evidence is supplied; all numeric values are heuristic priors.
Scope follows the framing of Casella & Berger (2002), Wasserman (2004), Gelman et al. (2013), and Efron & Hastie (2016).
exclusions: Causal-inference identification design (DAGs, IV, RDD) beyond its inferential interface.
Specific regression/model families and their estimation algorithms in detail.
Experimental and survey design logistics, sampling-frame construction, and data collection.
Software implementation, probabilistic-programming internals, and data engineering.

competency_questions.question: Given a research question, what is the precise estimand, should it be approached by estimation, testing, or prediction, and how is it pre-specified to avoid post hoc drift?
competency_questions.acceptance_condition: INFER_GOAL_FRAME maps the question to a pre-specified estimand and inference mode

competency_questions.question: Which point estimator is appropriate and how is its bias, variance, and efficiency characterized via the likelihood?
competency_questions.acceptance_condition: POINT_EST and LIKELIHOOD present with properties

competency_questions.question: How is a confidence interval constructed and why is it not a probability statement about the parameter?
How is a hypothesis test set up and what does its p-value actually mean?
How are p-hacking and selective reporting detected and prevented in the reported inference?
How does the likelihood unify frequentist and Bayesian inference?
How is a prior chosen and justified, and how are credible intervals interpreted from the posterior?
How is evidence between competing models quantified (Bayes factors vs information criteria) and why does the prior matter?
How is the magnitude of an effect estimated and reported as distinct from statistical significance?
Is the study adequately powered for the smallest meaningful effect, and why is observed power invalid?
How is error inflation controlled when many hypotheses are tested (FWER vs FDR)?
When should resampling (bootstrap vs permutation) be used, how is out-of-sample error estimated without leakage, and what are the validity conditions?
How is model complexity controlled through selection and regularization, and what does that cost downstream inference?
How are the assumptions an inference rests on checked and reported honestly so the result is reproducible?

glossary.definition: the precise population quantity an analysis aims to estimate
probability of a test statistic at least as extreme as observed if the null is true
an interval from a procedure with stated long-run coverage of the parameter
a posterior interval containing the parameter with stated posterior probability
the probability of the observed data viewed as a function of the parameters
a probability distribution over parameters before observing the data
the ratio of marginal likelihoods quantifying relative evidence between models
probability of rejecting the null when a specified alternative is true
probability of at least one false rejection across a family of tests
expected proportion of false rejections among all rejections
resampling the data to approximate a statistic's sampling distribution
held-out resampling to estimate out-of-sample predictive error
penalizing model complexity to trade bias for reduced variance
a quantitative measure of the magnitude of a phenomenon

evidence_label_policy.note: No observed/experimental inputs supplied; only heuristic labels are eligible.

source_registry.description: Heuristic priors from established statistical-inference literature (e.g., Casella & Berger 2002; Wasserman 2004; Gelman et al. 2013; Efron & Hastie 2016) and methodological practice; no measured dataset supplied.
grounding_limits: all numeric values are heuristic priors, not measurements
no observed or experimentally_validated labels are eligible

normalization_definitions.rounding: round computed scores to 2 decimals; tolerance 0.02

nodes.definition: Translate the substantive question into a precise inferential target (estimand, hypothesis, or predictive quantity) and choose estimation, testing, or prediction as the governing mode.

included: estimation vs testing vs prediction choice

contradictors: analyst who runs tests before defining the estimand

probabilistic_layer.update_signal: when the question shifts from estimating a magnitude to deciding between hypotheses or to out-of-sample prediction

pros.claim: every downstream method inherits validity from a correctly specified estimand
pros.example: asking 'how large is the effect' (estimation) versus 'is there any effect' (test) selects different tools

cons.claim: a vague or post hoc estimand invites the garden of forking paths and invalid inference
cons.example: redefining the outcome after seeing results inflates the false-positive rate

failure_modes: testing used where an interval estimate was needed
acceptance_tests: estimand is stated as a population quantity before analysis
inference mode (estimate/test/predict) is justified against the decision

nodes.definition: Construct frequentist point estimators (MLE, method of moments, plug-in/M-estimators) and characterize their bias, variance, consistency, and efficiency.

included: standard errors via Fisher information or sandwich

contradictors: practitioner who reports an estimate with no uncertainty

probabilistic_layer.update_signal: when the estimator's regularity assumptions (identifiability, smoothness) are violated

pros.claim: MLE is asymptotically efficient and gives a principled variance via Fisher information
pros.example: logistic-regression coefficients are MLEs with model-based standard errors

cons.claim: point estimates without standard errors are uninterpretable and MLE can be badly biased in small samples
cons.example: a small-sample odds-ratio MLE can be severely biased or infinite under separation

failure_modes: reporting an estimate without a standard error
acceptance_tests: a standard error or sampling-variance estimate accompanies every point estimate

nodes.definition: Construct and interpret frequentist confidence intervals (Wald, profile-likelihood, exact, bootstrap-based) with correct frequentist coverage semantics.

included: interpretation as a procedure with coverage

contradictors: analyst who reads a 95% CI as a 95% probability the parameter lies inside

probabilistic_layer.update_signal: when coverage is questioned by simulation or when intervals must replace p-values in reporting

pros.claim: intervals communicate magnitude and precision, not just a yes/no decision
pros.example: a CI of [0.1, 2.0] signals an imprecise estimate even when 'significant'

cons.claim: frequentist coverage is a property of the procedure, not a probability about the parameter, and Wald intervals can undercover
cons.example: a Wald binomial interval near p=0 has poor coverage; Wilson or exact is preferred

failure_modes: interpreting a CI as a posterior probability
using Wald where coverage is poor
acceptance_tests: interval interpretation states coverage of the procedure, not parameter probability
interval method chosen for adequate coverage in the regime

nodes.definition: Set up and run frequentist significance and Neyman-Pearson tests: null and alternative, test statistic, Type I/II error control, and the decision rule.

included: Type I/Type II error and alpha

contradictors: analyst who treats failure to reject as proof of the null

probabilistic_layer.update_signal: when the alpha level, sidedness, or null specification is challenged

pros.claim: provides a calibrated long-run error rate for a pre-specified decision
pros.example: a two-sample t-test controls Type I error at alpha when assumptions hold

cons.claim: non-significance is not evidence of no effect, and fixed-alpha thinking encourages dichotomania
cons.example: p=0.06 declared 'no effect' discards a possibly real but imprecisely estimated signal

acceptance_tests: null, alternative, and alpha are pre-specified
non-rejection is not interpreted as proof of the null

nodes.definition: Interpret p-values correctly and avoid the misinterpretations flagged by the ASA statement (probability of the null, effect size, replication probability).

included: definition as a tail probability under the null
p-value vs effect size vs evidence

contradictors: researcher who equates p<0.05 with an important or true effect

probabilistic_layer.update_signal: when a p-value drives a publication or policy claim, or when selective analysis is suspected

pros.claim: naming the precise meaning blocks the most damaging inferential errors
pros.example: a p-value is P(data this extreme or more | null true), not P(null true | data)

cons.claim: p-values are easily gamed and say nothing about magnitude or importance
cons.example: thresholding many comparisons at 0.05 manufactures false 'discoveries'

failure_modes: p equated with the probability the null is true
large p taken as proof of the null
ignoring multiplicity behind a reported p
acceptance_tests: interpretation explicitly avoids the ASA-listed fallacies
the p-value is reported with effect size and uncertainty
revisit_triggers: claim rests solely on a p-value threshold

nodes.definition: Use the likelihood function as the common engine for estimation and evidence: likelihood ratios, the likelihood principle, profile/marginal likelihood, and information.
contradictors: pure-significance tester who ignores the likelihood principle

probabilistic_layer.update_signal: when the model family changes or when frequentist and Bayesian uses of the likelihood are contrasted

pros.claim: unifies MLE, likelihood-ratio tests, and the Bayesian update under one object
pros.example: the same log-likelihood drives an MLE and, times a prior, a posterior

cons.claim: likelihood-based inference is only as valid as the assumed model family
cons.example: a misspecified likelihood yields confidently wrong information-based standard errors

failure_modes: treating a misspecified likelihood as exact
acceptance_tests: the likelihood is stated explicitly and its model assumptions are recorded

nodes.definition: Combine a prior with the likelihood via Bayes' theorem to obtain a posterior distribution and base estimation and decisions on it.
contradictors: strict frequentist who rejects any prior

probabilistic_layer.update_signal: when prior sensitivity or computational convergence is questioned

pros.claim: yields full probability statements about parameters and propagates uncertainty coherently
pros.example: a posterior gives P(theta>0 | data) directly, which a frequentist CI cannot

cons.claim: results depend on the prior and on computation that can fail to converge
cons.example: an over-informative prior can dominate weak data and bias the posterior

failure_modes: non-converged MCMC reported as a posterior
acceptance_tests: the posterior is reported with a prior-sensitivity check
computation diagnostics (e.g. R-hat) pass

nodes.definition: Choose and justify priors (informative, weakly-informative, reference/objective) and assess their influence through prior-sensitivity analysis.

included: informative vs weakly-informative vs reference priors

contradictors: analyst who claims a prior is 'objective' and beyond scrutiny

probabilistic_layer.update_signal: when results prove sensitive to the prior or when an informative prior must be defended

pros.claim: weakly-informative priors regularize and prevent absurd estimates
pros.example: a normal(0, 2.5) prior on logistic coefficients tames separation

cons.claim: a poorly chosen prior can dominate the data or smuggle in unwarranted certainty
cons.example: a tight prior centered on a wrong value biases the posterior away from the truth

failure_modes: flat prior treated as non-informative when it is not
acceptance_tests: the prior choice is justified and a sensitivity analysis is reported
prior predictive draws are plausible

nodes.definition: Summarize the posterior with credible intervals (equal-tailed or highest-posterior-density) and interpret them as direct probability statements about the parameter.
contradictors: analyst who conflates a credible interval with a confidence interval

probabilistic_layer.update_signal: when the difference between credible and confidence intervals matters for reporting

pros.claim: supports the intuitive statement people wrongly attach to confidence intervals
pros.example: a 95% HPD interval does mean 95% posterior probability the parameter lies inside

cons.claim: its validity depends entirely on the prior and model being defensible
cons.example: a credible interval inherits any bias from an over-informative prior

failure_modes: reporting a credible interval without noting prior dependence
confusing HPD with equal-tailed under skew
acceptance_tests: interpretation states posterior probability and notes prior dependence

nodes.definition: Quantify relative evidence between models or hypotheses with Bayes factors and posterior model probabilities, accounting for their sensitivity to priors.

included: Bayes-factor definition and the Jeffreys scale
sensitivity to the parameter prior (Lindley's paradox)

contradictors: NHST advocate who rejects a model-evidence framing

probabilistic_layer.update_signal: when the marginal likelihood is hard to compute or when the parameter prior drives the result

pros.claim: directly quantifies evidence for the null as well as the alternative, unlike p-values
pros.example: a Bayes factor near 1 says the data barely distinguish the hypotheses

cons.claim: Bayes factors are acutely sensitive to the parameter prior and computationally fragile
cons.example: Lindley's paradox: a diffuse prior makes a Bayes factor favor the null even when a test rejects it

acceptance_tests: the Bayes factor is reported with explicit parameter priors and a sensitivity check
the marginal-likelihood computation is validated

nodes.definition: Estimate, standardize, and report effect sizes (raw and standardized) with uncertainty, shifting interpretation from significance to magnitude.

included: raw vs standardized effect sizes (d, r, OR, RR)

contradictors: analyst who reports only p-values and no magnitude

probabilistic_layer.update_signal: when magnitude rather than mere detection drives the decision

pros.claim: makes results comparable and interpretable in terms of real-world importance
pros.example: Cohen's d=0.2 flags a small effect even if p is tiny in a huge sample

cons.claim: standardized effect sizes can mislead across different populations and scales
cons.example: the same d means different things when outcome variances differ across studies

acceptance_tests: an effect size with a confidence interval accompanies every key result

nodes.definition: Reason about statistical power and sample size for a smallest meaningful effect before data collection, and avoid post hoc observed power.

included: sample-size determination for a target effect
why post hoc observed power is invalid

contradictors: analyst who computes observed power to explain a null result

probabilistic_layer.update_signal: when the assumed effect size or variance proves wrong, or the design changes

pros.claim: prevents underpowered studies that cannot detect meaningful effects
pros.example: an a priori power analysis sizes a trial to detect the minimal important difference

cons.claim: power depends on an assumed effect size and variance that are often guessed, and post hoc power is circular
cons.example: using the observed effect as the target makes 'observed power' a deterministic function of the p-value

acceptance_tests: sample size justified against a pre-specified smallest meaningful effect
post hoc observed power is not used to interpret a null

nodes.definition: Control error inflation across many tests using family-wise error-rate (Bonferroni/Holm) or false-discovery-rate (Benjamini-Hochberg) procedures.
contradictors: analyst who runs dozens of tests and reports only the significant ones

probabilistic_layer.update_signal: when the number or family of tests changes, or when discovery vs confirmation goals shift

pros.claim: prevents a flood of false positives when many hypotheses are examined
pros.example: Benjamini-Hochberg controls FDR at 5% across thousands of genomic tests

cons.claim: over-correcting (FWER) can kill power, and the family definition is a judgment call
cons.example: Bonferroni across 10000 tests can make almost nothing detectable

failure_modes: no multiplicity adjustment for many tests
post hoc family definition to pass a threshold
wrong error rate for the goal
acceptance_tests: the test family is pre-specified and an appropriate FWER or FDR procedure is applied

nodes.definition: Use the bootstrap to approximate sampling distributions, standard errors, and confidence intervals by resampling the data when analytic formulas are unavailable.
contradictors: analyst who assumes the bootstrap always works

probabilistic_layer.update_signal: when data dependence or heavy tails threaten bootstrap validity

pros.claim: gives uncertainty estimates with minimal distributional assumptions
pros.example: a BCa bootstrap CI for a median needs no closed-form variance

cons.claim: fails for dependent data, extremes, and small samples, and can be silently wrong
cons.example: bootstrapping the maximum of a sample gives an inconsistent distribution

failure_modes: bootstrapping dependent data without a block scheme
acceptance_tests: bootstrap assumptions (iid or block structure) are checked before reporting

nodes.definition: Build exact or randomization tests by permuting labels under an exchangeability null, giving distribution-free p-values for sharp hypotheses.
contradictors: analyst who permutes when exchangeability does not hold

probabilistic_layer.update_signal: when the exchangeability assumption under the null is questioned

pros.claim: yields a valid distribution-free test of a sharp null without parametric assumptions
pros.example: permuting treatment labels tests a randomized experiment exactly

cons.claim: validity hinges on exchangeability under the null, which can be subtle
cons.example: permutation in clustered data without respecting clusters invalidates the p-value

failure_modes: testing a weak null with a sharp-null procedure
acceptance_tests: the exchangeability/null structure justifying permutation is stated
revisit_triggers: null reframed from sharp to weak

nodes.definition: Use cross-validation and held-out resampling to estimate out-of-sample predictive error and to tune and compare models honestly.

included: nested CV for tuning plus evaluation

contradictors: analyst who tunes and evaluates on the same fold

probabilistic_layer.update_signal: when leakage is suspected or when CV-based selection must be separated from evaluation

pros.claim: estimates generalization error without a separate test set and guards against overfitting
pros.example: nested CV separates hyperparameter tuning from honest performance estimation

cons.claim: leakage and dependent data make CV optimistic, and CV-based selection needs an outer loop
cons.example: scaling on the full dataset before CV leaks test information and inflates accuracy

failure_modes: tuning and evaluating on the same split
acceptance_tests: evaluation is on data not used for any tuning or preprocessing decision
fold structure respects dependence

nodes.definition: Compare and select models with information criteria (AIC, BIC, WAIC, cross-validated deviance), trading goodness of fit against complexity.
contradictors: analyst who selects a model then reports naive p-values from it

probabilistic_layer.update_signal: when AIC and BIC disagree or when post-selection inference validity is questioned

pros.claim: gives a principled, computable tradeoff between fit and parsimony
pros.example: AIC targets predictive accuracy while BIC targets the true model under its assumptions

cons.claim: selection invalidates downstream naive inference, and AIC and BIC encode different goals
cons.example: reporting confidence intervals from a selected model ignores selection uncertainty

failure_modes: comparing non-nested models on different data
acceptance_tests: the selection criterion matches the goal (prediction vs identification) and post-selection caveats are stated

nodes.definition: Apply penalized estimation (ridge, lasso, elastic net, hierarchical shrinkage) to trade bias for variance and stabilize estimation in high dimensions.
contradictors: analyst who reads lasso-selected variables as unbiased causal effects

probabilistic_layer.update_signal: when the penalty must be retuned or when shrinkage bias affects the inferential claim

pros.claim: controls overfitting and enables estimation when predictors outnumber observations
pros.example: ridge regression stabilizes coefficients under multicollinearity

cons.claim: introduces deliberate bias and complicates inference on individual coefficients
cons.example: lasso coefficient estimates are biased and their selection is unstable across resamples

failure_modes: over- or under-regularizing via a bad penalty
acceptance_tests: the penalty is tuned by an honest out-of-sample procedure and shrinkage bias is acknowledged

nodes.definition: Verify the modeling assumptions an inference rests on (distribution, independence, homoscedasticity) and assess robustness to violations.
contradictors: analyst who runs a parametric test without checking its assumptions

probabilistic_layer.update_signal: when diagnostics reveal violated assumptions affecting the inference

pros.claim: catches misspecification before it corrupts every downstream inference
pros.example: a residual plot reveals heteroscedasticity that invalidates model-based standard errors

cons.claim: diagnostics can be over- or under-interpreted and rarely prove a model correct
cons.example: passing a normality test in a tiny sample does not establish normality

failure_modes: over-trusting a single test of assumptions
acceptance_tests: key assumptions are checked and a robust alternative is used or justified when they fail

nodes.definition: Report estimates, uncertainty, assumptions, and analytic choices transparently, including pre-registration and the multiplicity of the analysis path.

included: reporting estimate plus interval plus assumptions

contradictors: analyst who reports only the most favorable analysis

probabilistic_layer.update_signal: when results are prepared for dissemination or when undisclosed analytic flexibility is detected

pros.claim: honest uncertainty reporting is the gate against irreproducible claims
pros.example: sharing all pre-registered and exploratory analyses lets readers calibrate the evidence

cons.claim: full transparency can expose messy, inconclusive results that pressure favors hiding
cons.example: reporting every specification may weaken a tidy narrative but is what integrity requires

acceptance_tests: estimate, uncertainty, assumptions, and analytic choices are all disclosed
deviations from pre-registration are logged
revisit_triggers: results move to publication or policy

edges.why_related: the estimand and inference mode determine which estimator is meaningful
edges.benefit_of_coupling: keeps estimation tied to a defined target
edges.risk_of_conflict: weak only if estimation precedes a fixed estimand
edges.example: an estimator is chosen once the estimand is a population quantity
edges.resolution_rule: estimand framing dominates estimator choice

edges.why_related: MLE and information-based standard errors are defined through the likelihood
edges.benefit_of_coupling: gives a principled variance and efficiency
edges.example: Fisher information from the log-likelihood yields the MLE variance
edges.resolution_rule: likelihood specification precedes estimator derivation

edges.why_related: intervals are built around a point estimate and its standard error
edges.example: a Wald CI uses the estimate plus or minus z times its SE
edges.resolution_rule: point estimate and SE are finalized before interval construction

edges.why_related: the hypotheses and decision mode come from the inferential framing
edges.risk_of_conflict: weak if hypotheses are set after seeing data
edges.example: a one-sided null follows from a directional pre-specified question
edges.resolution_rule: framing dominates; tests follow the pre-specified hypotheses

edges.why_related: a p-value only has meaning relative to a defined test and null
edges.example: p is interpreted relative to the stated null and alpha
edges.resolution_rule: interpretation must respect the test's construction

edges.why_related: the chosen model family fixes the likelihood used downstream
edges.example: specifying a logistic model fixes the binomial log-likelihood
edges.resolution_rule: model family is fixed during framing

edges.why_related: the posterior is the likelihood times the prior, normalized
edges.benefit_of_coupling: reuses one inferential object across paradigms
edges.example: the same log-likelihood enters the posterior kernel
edges.resolution_rule: likelihood is defined before Bayesian updating

edges.why_related: the posterior cannot be formed without a specified prior
edges.benefit_of_coupling: forces the prior to be justified up front
edges.risk_of_conflict: tension when the prior dominates weak data
edges.example: a weakly-informative prior is set before computing the posterior
edges.resolution_rule: prior is specified and sensitivity-checked before the posterior is finalized

edges.why_related: credible intervals are summaries of the posterior
edges.example: a 95% HPD interval is read off the posterior
edges.resolution_rule: posterior is validated before interval summaries

edges.why_related: Bayes factors compare marginal likelihoods from the Bayesian machinery
edges.example: posterior model probabilities follow from Bayes factors and model priors
edges.resolution_rule: marginal-likelihood computation is validated before reporting evidence

edges.why_related: effect-size reporting attaches a confidence interval to a magnitude
edges.benefit_of_coupling: shifts focus from significance to magnitude
edges.example: Cohen's d is reported with its CI
edges.resolution_rule: interval methods feed effect-size uncertainty

edges.why_related: power and sample size are computed for a target effect size
edges.benefit_of_coupling: sizes studies to detect meaningful effects
edges.risk_of_conflict: tension when the assumed effect is optimistic
edges.example: an a priori power analysis uses the minimal important difference
edges.resolution_rule: the target effect is set before sizing

edges.why_related: power is defined relative to the test's alpha and alternative
edges.benefit_of_coupling: ties design to the planned test
edges.risk_of_conflict: tension if observed power is misused
edges.example: power = 1 minus Type II error at the planned alpha
edges.resolution_rule: power reasoning uses a pre-specified test, not observed effects

edges.why_related: multiplicity control operates over a family of individual tests
edges.risk_of_conflict: tension between FWER strictness and power
edges.example: Benjamini-Hochberg adjusts a family of p-values
edges.resolution_rule: the test family is defined before correction

edges.why_related: the bootstrap resamples to get the sampling distribution of an estimator
edges.benefit_of_coupling: supplies standard errors without closed forms
edges.example: a BCa CI is bootstrapped for a complex estimator
edges.resolution_rule: the estimator/statistic is defined before resampling

edges.why_related: permutation builds an exact reference distribution for a test's null
edges.example: label permutation tests a sharp null exactly
edges.resolution_rule: the null and exchangeability structure are defined first

edges.why_related: cross-validation applies when the inferential goal is predictive accuracy
edges.benefit_of_coupling: matches method to a prediction goal
edges.risk_of_conflict: tension if leakage corrupts the estimate
edges.example: k-fold CV estimates out-of-sample error for a prediction task
edges.resolution_rule: predictive framing precedes CV-based evaluation

edges.why_related: cross-validated error is one basis for model selection alongside information criteria
edges.example: LOO-CV and WAIC both rank candidate models
edges.resolution_rule: selection criterion and goal are set before comparing models

edges.why_related: AIC and BIC are penalized log-likelihoods
edges.example: AIC = -2 log L + 2k from the fitted likelihood
edges.resolution_rule: the likelihood is fitted before computing criteria

edges.why_related: penalized estimation modifies the estimation objective with a complexity penalty
edges.example: ridge adds an L2 penalty to least squares
edges.resolution_rule: the base estimator/loss is defined before adding a penalty

edges.why_related: the regularization penalty is tuned by cross-validation
edges.risk_of_conflict: tension if tuning leaks into evaluation
edges.example: the lasso lambda is chosen by the CV one-SE rule
edges.resolution_rule: tuning is nested inside honest evaluation

edges.why_related: diagnostics validate the assumptions an estimator relies on
edges.example: residual plots check homoscedasticity behind a model SE
edges.resolution_rule: estimation assumptions are checked before inference is finalized

edges.why_related: a test's reference distribution is valid only if its assumptions hold
edges.example: a t-test assumes approximate normality of the mean
edges.resolution_rule: assumption checks gate the test's validity

edges.why_related: honest reporting requires effect sizes with their uncertainty
edges.risk_of_conflict: tension when transparency exposes weak results
edges.example: reporting d with its CI in the results section
edges.resolution_rule: reporting standards require magnitude plus uncertainty

edges.why_related: transparent reporting depends on correctly interpreting and disclosing p-values
edges.example: disclosing all tests behind a reported p-value
edges.resolution_rule: correct interpretation precedes disclosure

edges.why_related: Bayesian and frequentist paradigms give different inferential objects and can conflict on a claim
edges.benefit_of_coupling: clarifies which paradigm governs a decision
edges.risk_of_conflict: a result may be 'significant' yet have weak Bayesian evidence
edges.example: Lindley's paradox: a test rejects while a Bayes factor favors the null
edges.resolution_rule: pre-declare the inferential paradigm for the decision; if both are reported, reconcile via the pre-specified primary analysis

edges.why_related: strict multiplicity control lowers per-test power, conflicting with detection goals
edges.benefit_of_coupling: forces an explicit error-rate vs power tradeoff
edges.example: Bonferroni across many endpoints can require an infeasible sample size
edges.resolution_rule: use FDR rather than FWER when discovery is the goal, and pre-specify the primary endpoint

edges.why_related: shrinkage trades unbiasedness for lower variance, conflicting with unbiased estimation
edges.risk_of_conflict: shrunk coefficients are biased and can mislead inference
edges.example: lasso zeroes true-but-small coefficients, biasing effect estimates
edges.resolution_rule: prefer unpenalized estimation when unbiased inference on a coefficient is the goal; use shrinkage for prediction

edges.why_related: Bayes factors are acutely sensitive to the parameter prior, conflicting with stable conclusions
edges.benefit_of_coupling: exposes prior dependence of model evidence
edges.risk_of_conflict: a diffuse prior can flip the Bayes factor toward the null
edges.example: Lindley-Bartlett: vaguer parameter priors inflate evidence for the simpler model
edges.resolution_rule: require an explicit, defensible parameter prior and a sensitivity analysis before reporting a Bayes factor

edges.why_related: model selection creates selection uncertainty that naive reporting hides
edges.benefit_of_coupling: forces disclosure of post-selection inference limits
edges.risk_of_conflict: reporting CIs from a selected model understates uncertainty
edges.example: quoting a p-value from an AIC-selected model ignores the search
edges.resolution_rule: report selection uncertainty or use post-selection/averaging methods and disclose the selection procedure

edges.why_related: reusing the same CV to both tune the penalty and report error creates optimistic bias
edges.risk_of_conflict: a single CV used for both tuning and reporting overstates accuracy
edges.example: picking lambda and quoting that fold's error inflates performance
edges.resolution_rule: nest tuning inside an outer evaluation loop; never report the inner tuning score as the performance estimate

edges.why_related: framing the estimand early enables coherent honest reporting later
edges.risk_of_conflict: mild tension if framing is revised late
edges.example: a pre-registered estimand makes the final report straightforward
edges.resolution_rule: keep the estimand stable; if reframed, re-run reporting

edges.why_related: failed diagnostics trigger revisiting the estimator or its variance estimator
edges.example: heteroscedasticity prompts switching to sandwich standard errors
edges.resolution_rule: revisit estimation when diagnostics fail; stop after a robust alternative passes or after two iterations

edges.why_related: cross-validated error can trigger reconsidering the selected model
edges.benefit_of_coupling: keeps selection honest to out-of-sample performance
edges.risk_of_conflict: risk of overfitting the CV estimate by repeated selection
edges.example: a worse LOO score sends the analyst back to the candidate set
edges.resolution_rule: revisit selection on CV evidence; stop when the one-SE-rule model is stable or after a fixed number of rounds

edges.why_related: preparing the report can reveal that the original estimand was under-specified
edges.example: writing results exposes an ambiguous outcome definition
edges.resolution_rule: revisit framing when reporting reveals ambiguity; stop once the estimand is unambiguous and pre-registered

edges.why_related: both are resampling methods but answer different questions (variance vs sharp-null test)
edges.benefit_of_coupling: helps choose the right resampling tool
edges.risk_of_conflict: confusing the two leads to the wrong inference
edges.example: bootstrap for a CI, permutation for a test of no effect
edges.resolution_rule: use bootstrap for uncertainty of an estimate and permutation for a sharp-null test

edges.why_related: credible and confidence intervals look alike but have different interpretations
edges.benefit_of_coupling: prevents misreading one as the other
edges.risk_of_conflict: conflating them produces a wrong probability statement
edges.example: a 95% CI is not a 95% probability statement; a credible interval is
edges.resolution_rule: label each interval by its paradigm and interpret accordingly

conflict_axes.trigger: the same question is answered by both paradigms and they disagree on the conclusion
conflict_axes.dominance_logic: the pre-specified primary paradigm governs the headline claim; the other is reported as a sensitivity analysis
conflict_axes.escalation_threshold: paradigms disagree on a decision-relevant claim
conflict_axes.example: a test rejects the null while a Bayes factor favors it (Lindley's paradox)

conflict_axes.trigger: many tests require correction that drives per-test power below usefulness
conflict_axes.dominance_logic: for confirmatory primary endpoints use FWER; for discovery use FDR to preserve power
conflict_axes.escalation_threshold: correction makes the pre-specified primary endpoint underpowered
conflict_axes.example: Bonferroni over thousands of endpoints leaves nothing detectable

conflict_axes.trigger: shrinkage lowers variance but biases coefficients used for inference
conflict_axes.dominance_logic: use unpenalized estimation when unbiased coefficient inference is the goal; use shrinkage for prediction
conflict_axes.escalation_threshold: a shrunk coefficient is interpreted as an unbiased effect
conflict_axes.example: lasso zeroes a true small effect a study aimed to estimate

conflict_axes.trigger: an informative prior materially moves the posterior or Bayes factor
conflict_axes.dominance_logic: report prior-sensitivity; if conclusions flip across defensible priors, downgrade certainty
conflict_axes.example: a tight prior overrides weak but real data

conflict_axes.trigger: a significant result is trivially small or a non-significant result is practically large
conflict_axes.dominance_logic: magnitude with uncertainty governs the substantive claim; significance is necessary but not sufficient
conflict_axes.escalation_threshold: a tiny p with a negligible effect is presented as important
conflict_axes.example: p<0.001 for d=0.02 in a huge sample

conflict_axes.trigger: a more complex model fits better in-sample but generalizes worse
conflict_axes.dominance_logic: out-of-sample performance and the goal-matched criterion (AIC vs BIC) decide complexity
conflict_axes.escalation_threshold: in-sample fit chosen over a model with better predictive accuracy
conflict_axes.example: adding parameters lowers training deviance but raises CV error

conflict_axes.trigger: full disclosure of analytic flexibility weakens an otherwise tidy story
conflict_axes.dominance_logic: transparency dominates; all specifications and deviations are disclosed regardless of narrative cost
conflict_axes.escalation_threshold: selective reporting is tempting to preserve a headline claim
conflict_axes.example: only the significant specification is reported among many

conflict_axes.trigger: a convenient method's assumptions are doubtful for the data at hand
conflict_axes.dominance_logic: if key assumptions fail, switch to a robust or resampling alternative before reporting
conflict_axes.escalation_threshold: a parametric test is kept despite failed diagnostics
conflict_axes.example: a t-test is used on clearly skewed, dependent data

edge_cases.trigger: many analyses run, only significant ones reported
edge_cases.example: trying five outcome codings and reporting the one with p<0.05
edge_cases.detection_method: compare reported analyses against a pre-registration or analysis log; count undisclosed tests
resolution: require pre-registration
apply multiplicity control over the full family
disclose all analyses

edge_cases.trigger: an observational association is reported as a causal effect
edge_cases.example: a positive regression coefficient is described as the effect of X on Y without identification
edge_cases.detection_method: check whether a causal identification assumption is stated and defended
resolution: restate the claim as associational
or supply and defend an identification strategy

edge_cases.trigger: a confidence interval is interpreted as a posterior probability
edge_cases.example: claiming a 95% CI means a 95% chance the parameter is inside
edge_cases.detection_method: scan interpretation text for parameter-probability language attached to a frequentist CI
resolution: rephrase as coverage of the procedure
or compute a credible interval if a probability statement is wanted

edge_cases.trigger: observed power computed from the observed effect to explain a null
edge_cases.example: reporting 'observed power was 12% so the null is uninformative'
edge_cases.detection_method: detect use of the observed effect size as the power-analysis target after data are seen
resolution: replace with an a priori or sensitivity power analysis using a pre-specified effect

edge_cases.trigger: preprocessing or tuning uses information from held-out folds
edge_cases.example: standardizing on the full dataset before cross-validation
edge_cases.detection_method: audit the pipeline for any data-dependent step applied outside the training fold
resolution: move all fitting inside the training fold
use nested CV for tuning and evaluation

edge_cases.example: permuting individual labels in clustered data ignoring the clusters
edge_cases.detection_method: verify that the permuted units are exchangeable under the null
resolution: permute at the exchangeable level (e.g. clusters)
or use a model-based alternative

edge_cases.trigger: iid bootstrap applied to time series or extremes
edge_cases.example: bootstrapping autocorrelated returns with the ordinary bootstrap
edge_cases.detection_method: check the dependence structure and the statistic's tail behavior before bootstrapping
resolution: use a block bootstrap for dependence
avoid the bootstrap for extreme-value functionals

edge_cases.trigger: an over-informative prior dominates weak data
edge_cases.example: a tight prior centered off the truth pins the posterior away from the data
edge_cases.detection_method: run a prior-sensitivity analysis and compare to a weakly-informative prior
resolution: widen or re-justify the prior
report the sensitivity and downgrade certainty if conclusions flip

edge_cases.trigger: naive confidence intervals or p-values quoted after model selection
edge_cases.example: reporting standard CIs from a stepwise-selected model
edge_cases.detection_method: detect inference reported from a model chosen by a data-driven search without selection adjustment
resolution: use post-selection inference or sample splitting
or report model-averaged estimates

edge_cases.trigger: a numeric value carries an observed/experimentally_validated label without data
edge_cases.example: tagging a heuristic metric as 'observed' when no dataset exists
edge_cases.detection_method: scan all evidence labels against source_registry eligibility
resolution: downgrade the label to heuristic
reference SRC_HEURISTIC_PRIOR

edge_cases.trigger: a non-significant result is reported as proof of no effect
edge_cases.example: concluding 'no difference' from p=0.2 in an underpowered study
edge_cases.detection_method: check whether non-significance is paired with power/equivalence reasoning
resolution: report the confidence interval and power
use an equivalence test if absence of effect is the claim

workflow.objective: fix the estimand and inference mode
acceptance_tests: estimand stated as a population quantity
inference mode justified
workflow.do_first_because: all downstream validity is inherited from a correct estimand

workflow.objective: specify the model/likelihood and, if Bayesian, the prior
acceptance_tests: likelihood stated explicitly
prior justified and prior-predictive-checked when Bayesian
workflow.do_first_because: the likelihood and prior fix the engine for both estimation and Bayesian inference

workflow.objective: size the study for the smallest meaningful effect
acceptance_tests: sample size justified against a pre-specified effect
exit_criteria: design is adequately powered or explicitly exploratory
workflow.do_first_because: underpowered designs waste data and cannot detect meaningful effects

acceptance_tests: every estimate has a standard error
interval coverage is adequate
workflow.do_first_because: estimation precedes testing and effect-size reporting

workflow.objective: run tests, interpret p-values, control multiplicity
acceptance_tests: null/alpha pre-specified
multiplicity controlled for the family
p-values interpreted correctly
workflow.do_first_because: multiplicity must be handled before any p-value is interpreted as evidence

workflow.objective: compute the posterior and Bayesian summaries
acceptance_tests: computation diagnostics pass
prior sensitivity reported
workflow.do_first_because: Bayesian summaries need a validated posterior and a checked prior

workflow.objective: use resampling where analytic results are unavailable
acceptance_tests: bootstrap/permutation validity conditions checked
workflow.do_first_because: resampling validity (exchangeability, dependence) must be confirmed before use

acceptance_tests: no leakage across folds
selection criterion matches the goal
exit_criteria: model complexity is set with honest out-of-sample evidence
workflow.do_first_because: complexity must be chosen on out-of-sample evidence to avoid overfitting

workflow.objective: check assumptions and robustness across all inferences
acceptance_tests: key assumptions checked
robust alternative used or justified when they fail
workflow.do_first_because: diagnostics must pass before results can be locked

workflow.objective: report estimates, uncertainty, and analytic choices transparently
acceptance_tests: estimate, uncertainty, assumptions, and analytic choices disclosed
deviations logged
exit_criteria: the report is complete and disclosure-checked
workflow.do_first_because: honest disclosure is the final gate against irreproducible claims

priority_rationale.notes: every method inherits validity from the estimand
engine for MLE, criteria, and the Bayesian update
prior must exist before any posterior
estimates feed intervals, effect sizes, resampling
posterior feeds credible intervals and Bayes factors
controls false positives across the family
diagnostics gate locking of all inferences
out-of-sample basis for selection and tuning

dominance_rules.trigger: method chosen before the estimand is defined
dominance_rules.rule: the estimand and inference mode dominate tool selection
dominance_rules.required_action: define the estimand before selecting any estimator or test
dominance_rules.example: a causal estimand forbids reporting a bare association as the answer

dominance_rules.trigger: a high-value node depends on an unfinished prerequisite
dominance_rules.required_action: finalize prerequisites before dependent high-value work
dominance_rules.example: the posterior is not computed before the prior is specified

dominance_rules.trigger: a result is significant but trivially small or large but non-significant
dominance_rules.rule: effect magnitude with uncertainty dominates a significance verdict
dominance_rules.required_action: report effect size and CI alongside any significance claim
dominance_rules.example: p<0.001 with d=0.02 is reported as not practically important

dominance_rules.trigger: many tests reported without multiplicity control
dominance_rules.rule: multiplicity control over the test family dominates raw per-test p-values
dominance_rules.required_action: apply FWER or FDR over the pre-specified family
dominance_rules.example: thousands of genomic tests are reported under FDR, not raw 0.05

dominance_rules.trigger: results ready to lock but assumptions unchecked
dominance_rules.rule: assumption and robustness checks dominate locking results
dominance_rules.required_action: pass diagnostics before any result is hard-locked
dominance_rules.example: a model SE is not reported until residual diagnostics pass

dominance_rules.required_action: disclose all specifications, deviations, and analytic flexibility
dominance_rules.example: every pre-registered and exploratory analysis is reported

dominance_rules.trigger: a complex model fits better in-sample
dominance_rules.rule: honest out-of-sample evidence dominates in-sample fit
dominance_rules.required_action: choose complexity by cross-validated or goal-matched criteria
dominance_rules.example: a model with lower CV error is preferred over a better-fitting larger model

dominance_rules.trigger: a numeric value is labeled beyond its evidentiary support
dominance_rules.required_action: downgrade any non-heuristic label lacking an eligible source
dominance_rules.example: a heuristic metric is never labeled observed without a dataset

dominance_rules.trigger: risk_if_wrong>=0.80 or a paradigm/prior conflict is unresolved
dominance_rules.rule: human review dominates automation for high-risk inferential decisions
dominance_rules.required_action: escalate to human review before irreversible claims
dominance_rules.example: a causal or policy claim is human-reviewed before dissemination

anti_rework_rules.rule: do not select estimators or tests before the estimand is fixed
anti_rework_rules.rationale: a wrong estimand invalidates every downstream choice
anti_rework_rules.violation_signal: an estimator chosen with no written estimand
anti_rework_rules.example: picking a t-test before deciding the target quantity

anti_rework_rules.rule: do not finalize hypotheses, alpha, or the test family after seeing the data
anti_rework_rules.rationale: post hoc specification inflates false positives
anti_rework_rules.violation_signal: alpha or sidedness set after the result is known
anti_rework_rules.example: choosing one-sided after seeing the direction

anti_rework_rules.rule: do not compute the posterior before the prior is specified and checked
anti_rework_rules.rationale: an unjustified prior forces a full Bayesian redo
anti_rework_rules.violation_signal: a posterior reported with no prior justification
anti_rework_rules.example: running MCMC before writing down the prior

anti_rework_rules.rule: do not collect data before a power/sample-size justification
anti_rework_rules.rationale: an underpowered study cannot be salvaged after collection
anti_rework_rules.violation_signal: data collected with no sample-size rationale
anti_rework_rules.example: launching a trial without a power analysis

anti_rework_rules.rule: do not interpret p-values before defining the test family and correction
anti_rework_rules.violation_signal: significant findings reported with no family defined
anti_rework_rules.example: cherry-picking the smallest of many p-values

anti_rework_rules.rule: do not lock results before assumption and robustness checks pass
anti_rework_rules.rationale: locking on violated assumptions forces a redo
anti_rework_rules.violation_signal: results finalized with failing residual diagnostics
anti_rework_rules.example: reporting a model SE despite clear heteroscedasticity

anti_rework_rules.rule: do not report CV performance before confirming no leakage
anti_rework_rules.violation_signal: preprocessing fit on the full dataset before CV
anti_rework_rules.example: scaling features outside the training fold

anti_rework_rules.rule: do not report a Bayes factor before a parameter-prior sensitivity analysis
anti_rework_rules.rationale: prior-sensitive Bayes factors mislead and need redoing
anti_rework_rules.violation_signal: a single Bayes factor reported under one diffuse prior
anti_rework_rules.example: ignoring Lindley's paradox in model evidence

anti_rework_rules.rule: do not finalize the report before disclosing all analytic choices and deviations
anti_rework_rules.violation_signal: only the favorable specification appears in the report

iteration_protocol.trigger: validation report has any failed check
action: route each to its repair owner
acceptance_tests: every failed check is mapped to a repair route

iteration_protocol.detection: rank by risk and downstream impact
action: sort defects by risk_if_wrong and coupling
acceptance_tests: highest-risk defects are addressed first
iteration_protocol.stop_condition: queue empty or only sub-threshold defects remain

iteration_protocol.trigger: a defect is assigned to a subsystem
acceptance_tests: the targeted check passes after repair
formula.consistency passes within tolerance

iteration_protocol.trigger: new framing or sensitivity result changes importance
acceptance_tests: posterior matches the no-observed-data formula
iteration_protocol.stop_condition: posterior change below the revisit delta

iteration_protocol.trigger: unresolved high-risk defect or paradigm/prior conflict
action: open a human-review record with the decision and risk
acceptance_tests: a decision record with approver and risk acceptance exists

iteration_protocol.trigger: a new KB version is produced
iteration_protocol.detection: compare counts and pass-rate against the prior version
action: diff counts and failed-check ids against the baseline
acceptance_tests: no regression in pass-rate or required counts

checks.expected: labels legal and no observed without data

expected_properties: POINT_EST and INTERVAL_EST produced with SE

test_cases.input_summary: Bayesian analysis with an informative prior
expected_properties: prior-sensitivity reported before any Bayes factor

test_cases.input_summary: predictive model needing tuning and evaluation
expected_properties: nested CV separates tuning from evaluation

version_increment_rules: increment on any node addition/removal or formula change
increment on hard-lock of the report
lock_downgrade_rules: downgrade to draft when an upstream dependency changes
human_approval_required_for: resolving a paradigm or prior conflict
